For the checkpoint-only change before that rebase, see the [comparison against the prerequisite branch](https://github.com/MuskanPaliwal/cli/compare/refactor-git-metadata-owner...refactor-checkpoint-metadata-resolution).

Refs #2052 and #2190.

PR #2190 established the broader direction: physical Git worktree metadata should have one canonical owner instead of being rediscovered independently across the CLI. PR #2241 introduces that owner in `gitrepo` and migrates repository opening. This PR follows it by moving the checkpoint subsystem onto the canonical metadata boundary and deleting checkpoint's duplicate traversal and caching implementation.

This is intended as an ownership refactor rather than a checkpoint behavior change. Queue placement, redaction caching, persistent refs, shadow refs, locking, and caller-specific failure policies remain intact.

## Broader refactor

Checkpoint operations need to know both the current worktree root and the repository's common Git directory. The common directory determines where repository-wide state such as the push queue and redaction cache belongs, particularly when a command runs from a linked worktree.

Before this change, checkpoint resolved that metadata itself:

```text
Checkpoint operation
        │
        ▼
checkpoint.resolveGitCommonDir
        │
        ├── git rev-parse --git-common-dir
        ├── package-level mutex
        └── per-worktree cache
```

That made checkpoint a second owner of the same physical Git facts already being consolidated under `gitrepo`. It also gave checkpoint its own cache lifecycle, cancellation-dependent behavior, and subprocess cost.

After this change, checkpoint starts from the already-open repository and delegates physical metadata resolution to the canonical owner:

```text
Checkpoint operation
        │
        ▼
checkpoint.repositoryDirs
        │
        ▼
gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata
        │
        ├── Worktree root
        ├── Per-worktree Git directory
        └── Common Git directory
```

The checkpoint package retains a small adapter because checkpoint callers commonly need the worktree root and common directory together. Interpretation of `.git`, `gitdir:`, `commondir`, and linked-worktree layout remains owned exclusively by `gitrepo`.

## Why remove the checkpoint cache

The deleted cache was compensating for a Git subprocess rather than caching an expensive domain object. Once metadata resolution becomes rooted filesystem inspection, the cache no longer provides a useful ownership boundary.

Removing it has three useful consequences:

- An already-open repository no longer launches `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` when constructing checkpoint state.
- Repairs to `.git` or `commondir` metadata are observed by the next operation instead of remaining hidden behind a stale cached result.
- Checkpoint no longer owns a mutex, cache-clearing API, or cancellation-dependent cache semantics for facts owned by `gitrepo`.

This also removes the checkpoint-specific resolver and its cache-only tests.

## Checkpoint consumers moved to the canonical boundary

The migration covers the checkpoint paths that depend on repository metadata:

- rooted push-queue construction
- redaction-cache placement
- persistent ref updates
- ref-store construction
- ephemeral checkpoint storage
- shadow-ref operations
- file-lock placement

These consumers now receive metadata from the same resolver used when opening the repository, without introducing a generic Git facade or moving checkpoint-specific policy into `gitrepo`.

## Caller policy remains local

The canonical resolver reports metadata facts and errors; it does not decide whether an individual checkpoint feature is required or optional.

That distinction remains deliberate:

- Push-queue construction fails closed because enqueueing against the wrong repository directory could lose or misdirect required work.
- Redaction caching fails open because caching is an optimization and transcript redaction can continue without it.
- Persistent ref updates retain their existing locking, compare-and-swap conflict handling, retry, and cancellation behavior.
- Linked worktrees continue sharing repository-wide state through the common Git directory.
- Shadow refs and ephemeral checkpoint data retain their existing worktree-specific placement.

## Observable effect

No user-facing command or checkpoint format changes.

The operational effect is narrower:

- checkpoint metadata lookup no longer launches a Git subprocess for an already-open repository
- checkpoint metadata is no longer memoized independently from the filesystem
- malformed metadata continues to follow each caller's existing required or optional failure policy
- ordinary repositories and linked worktrees retain their existing storage locations

The checkpoint-only layer relative to #2241 contains 16 files, with 139 additions and 211 deletions. Most additions are focused behavioral tests; the production change primarily removes duplicate traversal and cache machinery.

## Verification

- `mise run check`
  - formatting passed
  - lint passed with 0 issues
  - race-enabled unit and integration tests passed
  - Vogon canary passed 56/56
  - external deterministic canary passed 4/4
- Pre-PR `mise run lint` passed with 0 issues.
- `git diff upstream/main...HEAD --check` passed.
- A real linked-worktree fixture proves that its queue is stored in the main repository's common Git directory.
- A repair test proves that corrected metadata is observed immediately without clearing a cache.
- A Git Trace2 test proves that constructing a checkpoint queue from an already-open repository launches no metadata Git subprocess.
- The Trace2 positive control runs `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` and confirms that the subprocess detector records it.
- Tests preserve the required queue fail-closed and optional redaction-cache fail-open policies.
- The repository ownership guard no longer needs an exception for checkpoint metadata traversal.
- Source-built `entire status` passed.
- Source-built `entire doctor` reported metadata branches and hooks as healthy; it also found two pre-existing ended sessions awaiting condensation, unrelated to this diff.

No paid real-agent E2E tests were run.

## Deliberately not included

This PR does not migrate session, strategy, hook, or other product consumers. Those areas have separate migrations so their error handling, fallback behavior, and performance-sensitive paths can be reviewed independently.

It also does not redesign checkpoint persistence, change ref formats, alter queue semantics, add cross-worktree writes, or replace genuine Git queries for refs, objects, configuration, and repository semantics.

{"body":"Fixes #2020.

Codex 0.149.0 can load project hooks from a different checkout than the one in which it is running. In a conventional linked worktree, its app-server `hooks/list` response reports the primary checkout's `.codex/hooks.json`; a divergent file present only in the linked worktree is not loaded.

This PR makes that effective location visible without giving Entire ownership of another checkout. Discovery and mutation are deliberately separate: Entire may inspect the file Codex actually loads, but installs, removes, and cleans hooks only in the exact checkout where the command was invoked.

## Discovery and ownership

- `WorktreeHooksPath` identifies `<current-checkout>/.codex/hooks.json`. It is the only mutation target used by install, uninstall, presence, freshness, deselection, and clean flows.
- `DiscoveredHooksPath` identifies the project hooks file Codex is expected to load. It is used only for read-only configuration and trust diagnostics.
- `ResolveHookDiscovery` consumes the shared `gitrepo.ResolveGitLayout` classification rather than maintaining a Codex-specific `.git`, `commondir`, or worktree-marker parser.
- Conventional linked worktrees discover the primary checkout's hook file. Normal checkouts, ordinary submodules, and separate-Git-directory checkouts discover their own hook file.
- `.bare/worktrees`, linked submodules, contradictory metadata, and other behavior not pinned against Codex are reported as unresolved. Entire does not claim an unsupported layout or guess a writable fallback.

`HookDiscovery` carries no write target, migration path, cleanup path, or lock path. Its `RepositoryWide` bit describes the reach of the configuration Codex discovers; it does not authorize repository-wide mutation.

## Checkout-local mutation

`entire enable`, `entire agent remove codex`, agent deselection, and `entire clean` mutate only the current checkout's `.codex/hooks.json`. They do not create another checkout's `.codex` directory, migrate a worktree-local file into the primary checkout, remove a discovered file owned elsewhere, or perform repository-wide cleanup.

Concurrent updates are serialized only with `<current-checkout>/.codex/hooks.json.lock`. There is no `entire-codex-hooks.lock` in the Git common directory and no synchronization across worktrees. An old common-directory lock, if present from a previous build, is neither used nor cleaned from another checkout.

Current-checkout writes are hardened before the final atomic replacement:

- the logical target must be exactly `<current-checkout>/.codex/hooks.json`;
- redirected `.codex` directories, final-file symlinks, non-regular files, unrelated destinations, and Git-metadata redirection are rejected;
- existing user hooks, unknown hook events, and unrelated top-level fields are preserved;
- uninstall removes only Entire-managed entries;
- an existing file keeps its permission bits, while a new file uses `0600`.

## Bounded read-only inspection

The local and discovered files are inspected independently as absent, user-only, Entire-managed, invalid, or unresolved. Inspection is contained to the exact canonical `.codex` directory, requires a stable regular file, caps `hooks.json` at 1 MiB, reads through a limit with one overflow byte, and checks file identity before and after the read. It never creates a directory, rewrites configuration, removes entries, or acquires a mutation lock.

The structured inspection also reports whether the core Entire events are present, which current events are missing, whether managed commands and timeouts match this CLI, whether the current checkout has the project layer Codex requires, whether local trust records were readable, and which declared hooks lack an approval record. Entire does not compute, copy, or synthesize Codex trust hashes.

## Diagnostics and remedy

- `entire doctor` reports the current-worktree path and Codex-discovered path, invalid or unresolved discovery, a missing project layer, managed hook drift, and trust gaps.
- `entire status` keeps current-checkout installation/freshness semantics separate from effective Codex discovery and exposes the mismatch under the existing `codex_hooks` JSON object without changing the warning wording established in this PR.
- SessionStart appends a short, bounded, read-only discovery or trust warning when applicable.

When hooks exist only in a linked worktree, Entire does not repair the primary checkout automatically. The user-owned remedy is to commit `.codex/hooks.json` and apply that commit to the primary checkout (typically by cherry-pick), or run `entire enable` from the primary checkout. Because linked worktrees share Git objects, the commit is immediately available to cherry-pick; no push or fetch is required.

## Pinned Codex integration contract

`TestCodexAppServerHooksList_LinkedWorktreeUsesPrimaryCheckout` is a no-model integration test pinned to `@openai/codex@0.149.0`. It:

1. creates a normal repository and conventional linked worktree with distinct hook markers;
2. starts `codex app-server` in the linked worktree with an isolated `CODEX_HOME`;
3. sends `initialize`, `initialized`, and `hooks/list` JSONL messages over stdio;
4. requires the primary marker and primary `sourcePath`;
5. rejects the linked-only marker; and
6. requires empty `warnings` and `errors`.

The test makes no model request and needs no OpenAI credentials. Local integration runs skip when the exact Codex binary is unavailable. CI installs version 0.149.0 and sets `ENTIRE_TEST_REQUIRE_CODEX_APP_SERVER=1`, so a missing binary or version drift fails rather than silently skipping.

## Verification status

The implementation includes focused unit coverage for Git-layout classification, path-role separation, current-checkout-only install/remove/clean behavior, exact-worktree locking, destination containment, symlink refusal, bounded reads, mode preservation, doctor/status/SessionStart diagnostics, trust inspection, and JSON output, plus the pinned app-server integration contract above.

Full formatting, lint, unit, integration, canary, duplication, and `mise run check` verification is intentionally deferred to implementation-order item 9.

{"body":"Refs #2091, item 3 only.

Before this change, Claude Code's Stop hook waited for a transcript sentinel that no longer appears, then fell back to a 500 ms quiet window. The wait only validated a mutable path. Lifecycle copied that path later, and provisional-checkpoint finalization opened it once more. Entire could therefore store bytes other than the ones it had treated as ready.

This PR replaces that sequence with one owned, validated snapshot for Claude Stop. Modern Claude payloads provide the final assistant response, so Entire can validate a transcript immediately with no artificial wait. Older payloads retain the 500 ms quiet-window fallback. The lifecycle also keeps checkpoints refreshable across Claude's repeatable Stop events and derives file and token metadata from one transcript parse.

## The wait did not own the transcript

TranscriptPreparer returns only an error. It gives the caller no bytes, open handle, identity, size, or file version. A successful wait says that path state A looked ready, but lifecycle can then copy state B and checkpoint finalization can read state C.

Shortening the wait alone would reduce latency while leaving that race intact. Valid final JSON would not be enough either: a complete older prefix can be syntactically valid even when the current turn has not reached the file.

## Owned, validated Stop snapshots

The built-in Claude Code adapter now has a Stop-specific capture operation. It:

1. fingerprints the producer-owned transcript by file identity, size, and modification time;
2. reads exactly the observed byte range;
3. verifies both the opened handle and current path still identify the observed file version;
4. validates the JSONL and derives the position from those exact bytes; and
5. returns an Entire-owned snapshot used by lifecycle, metadata analysis, position advancement, and checkpoint finalization.

None of those consumers reopens Claude's live transcript for the same Stop. If the file changes during capture, the bytes are discarded and capture retries against the new version.

The portable fingerprint catches ordinary appends, truncation, replacement, and rewrites whose modification time changes. It cannot prove that a same-size rewrite did not happen when the filesystem also reports the same timestamp. Claude appends transcript records, so that is an acceptable limit here; the tests do not claim stronger detection.

## Modern readiness is evidence-based and immediate

For modern payloads, non-empty last_assistant_message supplies current-turn evidence. Capture requires a transcript position successfully measured at TurnStart, reconstructs the latest assistant text only after that boundary, and requires it to match Claude's supplied final response.

The first readiness check now runs immediately. The previous design waited for the first 50 ms ticker event even when the transcript was already complete. After the immediate attempt, incomplete captures return to the normal 50 ms polling cadence.

A rejected file fingerprint is remembered. Entire does not reread and revalidate the same unchanged 70 MiB snapshot every 50 ms; it waits until file identity, size, or modification time provides new evidence.

Missing, stale, incomplete, continuously changing, mismatched, timed-out, and canceled captures return no snapshot. The maximum wait remains three seconds.

## Legacy payloads keep the quiet-window fallback

When last_assistant_message is missing, null, or empty, Entire has no producer evidence that the current final response reached the transcript. It therefore retains the 500 ms quiet window used by older Claude Code versions.

The split is intentional:

| Payload | Readiness evidence | Timing behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modern | Stable owned snapshot, valid current-turn JSONL, final response match | Immediate first check; 50 ms polling only when not ready |
| Legacy | Stable owned snapshot, structurally valid ending, 500 ms without file changes | Always pays the quiet window |

## Repeatable Claude Stops remain refreshable

A blocking Claude Stop hook can cause the same assistant turn to continue and later emit another Stop without a new UserPromptSubmit event. A valid last_assistant_message proves readiness for one Stop; it does not prove that Claude will never continue afterward.

Claude therefore advertises a repeatable turn-end capability. After each Stop, Entire:

- finalizes checkpoints using the validated snapshot available at that Stop;
- retains the original turn boundary and checkpoint IDs;
- tracks commits made during a continuation; and
- refreshes the same checkpoints if another Stop arrives.

The next user prompt or SessionEnd seals the turn. stop_hook_active is preserved as protocol metadata but is not treated as proof that a Stop is permanently final.

If the latest checkpoint refresh fails, Entire keeps the last successfully stored transcript and preserves the checkpoint IDs as recovery bookkeeping. Successful session-end refreshes release those IDs; failed ones keep the supporting shadow-branch state protected from cleanup.

## File and token analysis share one parse

Claude file extraction and token calculation previously implemented separate capabilities, each of which parsed the same main transcript and subagent transcripts independently.

The optional TranscriptTurnAnalyzer capability now parses the current main turn once and derives both modified files and token usage from those records. Each subagent transcript is likewise parsed once for both results. Other agents retain the existing independent capability fallback.

Capture validation remains a separate, lightweight safety pass. Its question is whether the bytes are safe and complete; turn analysis answers what metadata those validated bytes contain.

## Capture and analysis timing

These are medians from three runs on an Apple M3. They measure transcript capture, validation, and transcript-backed metadata analysis, not complete end-to-end Stop-hook latency.

### Modern Claude Stop hook

| Transcript case | Capture + validation | File/token analysis | Total transcript latency |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB normal turn | 0.170 ms | 0.249 ms | 0.419 ms |
| 4 MiB large turn | 8.848 ms | 15.966 ms | 24.814 ms |
| 70 MiB session, small current turn at tail | 13.134 ms | 19.308 ms | 32.442 ms |
| 70 MiB entirely belonging to current turn | 152.057 ms | 281.803 ms | 433.860 ms |

The realistic large-history case is the third row: the transcript file is 70 MiB, but most records belong to earlier turns. The 433.860 ms case deliberately makes all 70 MiB one enormous current turn.

### Legacy Claude Stop hook

| Transcript case | Capture including quiet window | Analysis | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB | 501.098 ms | 0.249 ms | 501.347 ms |
| 4 MiB | 501.653 ms | 15.966 ms | 517.619 ms |
| 70 MiB session, small tail turn | 514.228 ms | 19.308 ms | 533.536 ms |
| 70 MiB full current turn | 514.228 ms | 281.803 ms | 796.031 ms |

Other timing cases:

- A modern transcript that is already ready has no artificial wait.
- If writing finishes after Stop begins, latency is the remaining write delay plus approximately 50–100 ms stability detection and processing time.
- A transcript that never becomes valid, or whose final response never matches, times out after three seconds.
- Missing or already stale transcripts fail immediately.

The common modern case moves from the previous PR design's unavoidable 50 ms first poll to actual processing time: under 1 ms for a small transcript and about 32 ms for a realistic 70 MiB historical session.

## Test coverage

Focused tests cover:

- immediate modern capture independent of the poll interval;
- legacy quiet-window behavior and mid-write pauses;
- repeated assistant text before the current-turn boundary;
- partial final JSON and complete JSON without a trailing newline;
- continued growth, truncation, replacement, and same-size rewrites with changed modification time;
- remembered rejection of an unchanged snapshot;
- missing, stale, timed-out, and canceled capture;
- source mutation after capture and finalization ownership;
- measured-zero versus unmeasured-zero turn positions;
- repeated Stops reusing one turn boundary;
- commits and checkpoint refreshes during Stop continuations; and
- successful versus failed session-end refresh cleanup.

The benchmarks live in cmd/entire/cli/agent/claudecode/transcript_capture_test.go.

## Verification

Fresh verification for commit 40fbeb0c2:

- Required mise run check passed.
- Race-enabled unit and integration suite passed.
- Vogon canary passed 56/56.
- Roger-Roger canary passed 4/4.
- Post-commit mise run lint passed with 0 issues before push.
- git diff --check passed.

The separately reported test totals were:

- Unit: 9,740 tests, 5 skipped.
- Integration: 531 tests, 3 skipped.
- Lint: 0 issues.

## Kept out of this PR

This PR does not introduce a repository-wide TranscriptPreparer replacement, change external-agent readiness contracts, enforce a minimum Claude Code version, or claim end-to-end Stop-hook latency from the transcript-only benchmarks.

{"body":"this is the dedupe half of #1937, split into its own pr after @Soph asked to keep the gitrepo fix separate ([comment](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1937#issuecomment-5267402995)). the underlying report is entireio/cli#1927: a single checkpoint `metadata.json` grew to 111.79 MB, 94% of it `files_touched`, holding 1,292,257 entries of which only 67,340 were unique — a 19x duplication factor. once that blob crossed github's 100 MB limit, `entire/checkpoints/v1` became permanently unpushable, and the failure only surfaced as a warning tacked onto unrelated pushes.

## what this does

`writeSessionToSubdirectory` used to write `opts.FilesTouched` into the session metadata exactly as handed to it. it now runs the list through `NormalizeFilesTouched` first: dedupe, sort, normalize to forward slashes. on the issue's measured numbers that alone takes the blob from 111.79 MB to about 5.5 MB and back under the limit.

a few details that came out of review on #1937 (thanks @ecgang):

* the helper preserves nil-versus-empty. `files_touched` is marshaled without `omitempty`, so nil stays JSON `null` and a non-nil empty list stays `[]` — the wire format is unchanged for empty inputs.
* both live backends inherit the fix through the shared `treeWriter` (`gitRefsStore` embeds it), and the test now runs against both the git-branch and git-refs stores instead of leaning on the embedding argument.
* the fsstore reference backend applies the same normalization, since it's the worked example the next real backend would copy.

## why it warns instead of deduping silently

soph's worry on #1937 was that a silent dedupe hides the actual bug, and it's a fair worry: every merge path in the current code already dedupes — i audited them, and @ecgang audited them independently and came up equally empty (their comment on #1927 lists the paths) — so whatever produced the 19x duplication is either a version older than 0.8.42 or a path nobody has found yet. so when the boundary strips duplicates, it now logs a warning with the session id and the reported-versus-unique counts. if a live producer exists, it shows up in `.entire/logs` instead of disappearing into the dedupe.

## tests

* `TestWriteCommitted_DeduplicatesFilesTouched`: duplicated input written, permanent record read back deduplicated and sorted, against both git backends. fails without the boundary dedupe.
* empty-input cases pin the nil-versus-`[]` behavior.
* `mise run check` green: fmt, lint, unit, integration, and the e2e canary.

## what this does not do

it can't repair a branch that already carries an oversized blob — git history is immutable, so an affected `entire/checkpoints/v1` needs a one-time rewrite, as discussed on the issue. and it deliberately doesn't touch the nested-checkout walking, which is the other (unbounded) half of the issue and lives in #1937.

{"body":"Part 5 of #2190's [agreed split](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2190#issuecomment-5499945525), following the canonical resolver in #2241 and checkpoint migration in #2254.

This branch includes the session migration from #2285 and strategy migration from #2305. Both prerequisites remain open. Keep this PR **open** until they land, then refresh onto main so reviewers can assess the remaining-consumer changes separately.

### Why this change is needed

The earlier migrations introduced `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`, but several consumers still interpreted Git metadata through older code. Codex and status had their own traversal logic. Settings, review, investigation, and trail still depended on forwarding helpers or the common-directory resolver and cache.

Leaving those callers behind would preserve the disagreement this refactor is meant to remove. A caller could reuse a cached directory after metadata changed, or interpret a linked worktree differently from the session and checkpoint stores using the same repository.

This PR moves the remaining physical metadata lookups to the canonical resolver and deletes the old implementations after their final callers migrate.

### Metadata resolution and storage ownership

`gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata` supplies the per-worktree Git directory, common Git directory, and worktree ID for an explicit worktree root. It returns complete metadata or an error, without running Git or caching the result.

The remaining consumers use those facts for different purposes:

- Codex determines which checkout owns the discovered hook configuration. Its backlink, trust, submodule, and bare-layout checks remain consumer policy.
- Status reads HEAD from the per-worktree Git directory. Explain and cleanup use the resolved worktree ID when selecting checkpoint or shadow-branch state.
- Settings locates clone preferences in the common directory.
- Review and investigation locate their shared markers, manifests, and findings.
- Trail locates shared metadata and the base directory for checkout paths.
- Setup cleanup opens the common directory through the shared rooted API.

`paths.WorktreeRoot` still owns CWD discovery and its cache. `gitdir` still owns shared `os.Root` handles, including their lifetime and explicit reset behavior. Reads, writes, and locks continue through the existing rooted/no-follow storage code.

Git queries remain where their answer establishes repository membership, validates a reusable worktree, or inspects configuration and history. Replacing those queries with filesystem traversal would remove validation that the resolver does not provide.

### Failure behavior and printed paths

The tests exercise callers after a successful lookup, damage `commondir`, then repair it without clearing a metadata cache.

Required operations fail while metadata is broken. These include clone-preference writes, review marker and manifest writes, investigation-store construction, and cleanup preview. Optional callers retain their own behavior: status omits an unavailable branch, explain skips worktree filtering, settings skips an unresolved preferences layer, and trail refresh can still spawn when its throttle metadata cannot resolve. Repair restores access to the previously saved content.

Trail checkout also needs to preserve the path it prints. The first full verification run caught a regression where discovery changed macOS `/var` paths to `/private/var`. Trail now recovers the caller's spelling only after confirming that a CWD ancestor identifies the discovered root. Regression tests cover entry from both the checkout root and a nested directory.

### Legacy deletion and diff size

With the remaining callers migrated, this removes:

- `paths.GetWorktreeID` and its marker-based parser.
- The exported `ResolveDotGitPath` and `ResolveCommonGitPath` composition APIs and their old implementations.
- Session common-directory forwarding and cache-clearing APIs.
- The `gitdir` common-directory resolver/cache, obsolete resets, and cache-only tests.

The final ownership guard has no migration exceptions. It retains individually documented discovery, semantic-query, and policy exceptions, and fails when an exception becomes stale.

The part-5 commit changes 49 files: 18 production files, 30 tests, fixtures, or benchmarks, and one documentation file. Most test edits replace deleted APIs or remove obsolete cache resets. Production Go shrinks by 301 lines.

### Verification

The implementation's final `mise run check` passed, including race-enabled unit and integration tests, Vogon 56/56, and the external deterministic canary 4/4. A subsequent pre-push lint run passed with zero issues.

Independent review reran the focused migration tests with race detection, plus the full settings, investigation, and paths suites. Real Git fixtures cover eleven layouts, including ordinary and linked worktrees, bare-backed worktrees, separate Git directories, submodules, relative pointers, moved registrations, and aliases. Tests check actual stored files, recovery after metadata repair, rooted-handle lifetime, lock ordering and release, and printed trail paths.

Temporary source mutations confirmed that the ownership guard rejects independent traversal, a metadata query hidden behind a constant, and a stale exception.

The same Trace2 fixture was run against the integrated prerequisite baseline and this implementation:

| Operation | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Session construction from cold CWD | 1 | 1 |
| Session construction with an explicit root | 0 | 0 |
| Queue construction from an open repository | 0 | 0 |
| Prepare-commit with no session | 2 | 2 |
| Enabled text status with no session | 5 | 4 |
| Codex discovery from cold CWD | 1 | 1 |

These count Git subprocesses inside the named entry points. They do not measure full CLI startup or establish latency improvements.

Windows test binaries cross-compiled during implementation. Windows runtime testing and paid real-agent E2E tests were not performed.

  → canonical Git metadata identity
  → native atomic ref updates
  → storage batching and transcript snapshot consistency

- TECH: concurrent writers, symbolic refs, cancellation, error classification
- key distinction to remember:

  - OPF must reject a changed tip when that changes the meaning/base of the operation

## 4. previous work that connects naturally to Entire

### the overall collision

```text
Vibinex: infer useful context from Git history and code structure
Moss:    ingest, index, filter, rank, and retrieve information efficiently
Entire:  capture development context at creation time, bind it to Git,
         then make it searchable and usable by future humans and agents
```

★ Core answer:

> Entire feels less like a new domain and more like the convergence of the two domains I have already worked in. Vibinex taught me that a diff is not enough to understand a change. Moss taught me what it takes to ingest and retrieve useful information at scale. Entire captures the missing reasoning at the source, gives it durable Git provenance, and builds search, graph, review, and future agent workflows on top of it.

### Vibinex
- founding/product engineer in a three-person early-stage devtools startup; helped move from zero to 15+ customers
- built the **Git Profiler CLI in Rust**
- analyzed PRs / Git history to help teams understand changes and identify relevant reviewers
- worked on **syntactic diff graphs**, Git-blame relevance, authorship/reviewer signals
- built backend integrations around GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket
- designed privacy-conscious/on-prem processing when customers could not send source code to a hosted service
- worked directly with customers, so architecture and product feedback were never far apart
- recurring theme: **a code diff alone does not contain enough context to understand a change**
- ★ connection to Entire: Vibinex reconstructed context *after the fact* from code, blame, authorship, and repository history; Entire preserves much richer context *at creation time* and links it back to the same Git primitives

### Moss
- founding Rust/backend engineer working across Rust core, PyO3, Python/JS SDKs, and cloud ingestion services
- worked on an HNSW path for large embedding indexes, a compact binary embedding format, and bulk index creation through presigned object-store uploads
- shipped metadata filtering across Rust, PyO3, Python, and JS/TS surfaces, including comparison, set, boolean, and proximity operators
- found that post-filtering shallow `top_k` candidate lists destroyed hybrid-search recall; widened fusion depth, used union-based RRF, corrected score/filter ordering, and ran keyword/embedding branches in parallel
- measured filtered hybrid-search latency improving from roughly **88 ms → 17 ms on a 100k-document benchmark** while fixing empty-result quality failures
- built multi-document parsing/indexing and source-file tracking across doc-parser and index-manager flows
- moved embedding implementation and then orchestration toward Rust ownership: model download/cache, tokenization, ONNX inference, pooling, normalization, and session concurrency; verified numerical parity before deleting the Python implementation
- ★ connection to Entire: checkpoint history becomes a large, heterogeneous retrieval corpus; candidate recall, metadata filters, freshness, indexing ownership, latency, and honest partial results all matter
- accuracy note: this experience transfers directly to Entire Search concepts, but Entire's actual ANN/index implementation lives in backend repositories, not this CLI

### the three recurring engineering themes

1. **Provenance:** Vibinex asked who/what produced a change; Entire records the session and prompt that produced it.
2. **Retrieval:** Moss asked how to find the right information quickly and correctly; Entire Search asks that over code, commits, checkpoints, sessions, prompts, and transcripts.
3. **Trustworthy automation:** all three systems must distinguish absence from observation failure, preserve ownership boundaries, and recover honestly after interruption.

### recent platform / migration work
- worked across backend + infra + E2E workflows
- Java/Spring Boot + Next.js preview runtime / migration flows
- dealt with process lifecycle, health checks, ports, DB wiring, workspace VMs, Playwright E2E coverage
- also worked on code-review/eval behavior where **“no finding” must not accidentally mean “successful review”**
- connection: correctness under failure states / automation cannot collapse “failed to observe” into “nothing is wrong”

### Rust / systems
- EuroRust speaker: **“Production Unsafe Rust: Patterns for Zero-Copy Performance”**
- interested in systems, developer tools, low-level correctness, Git internals, and performance

## 1. my 60-second intro

> I am a backend and systems engineer who keeps gravitating toward developer tools, Git, search, and code intelligence. I spent roughly three years as a founding engineer at Vibinex, where I built a Rust CLI and backend systems for understanding pull requests through syntactic diff graphs, Git-blame relevance, authorship, and reviewer suggestions. At Moss, I moved deeper into search infrastructure: ANN performance, hybrid semantic and keyword retrieval, metadata filtering, bulk indexing, and moving embedding ownership into Rust. I started contributing to Entire because it joins those two worlds. Vibinex tried to recover context from code and Git history; Moss made large bodies of information fast and searchable; Entire preserves the reasoning behind code when it is created and then makes that history useful to humans and agents. Over the last few months I have contributed mostly around checkpoint correctness, Git refs, linked worktrees, session recovery, and transcript consistency.

### shorter, more conversational version

- backend / systems / devtools engineer; strongest interests are **Git, correctness, search, Rust, and developer tooling**
- built Git and PR-understanding tools at Vibinex, then search and indexing infrastructure at Moss
- now contributing deeply to Entire's checkpoint/session and Git-integration layers
- ★ throughline: **helping people and agents understand not only what code is present, but how and why it came to exist**
- ★ I learned Entire primarily by using it, reading the code, reproducing hard edge cases, and iterating through detailed reviews

### who I am beyond the resume

- grew up in Rajasthan and was the first daughter in my family to leave home to study computer science
- curiosity about what happens behind the "black box" of a computer has been a constant since childhood
- started an Entrepreneurship Cell in college, led a 20-person team, and placed fifth in IIT Bombay's National Entrepreneurship Challenge
- deliberately chose small startups and difficult, ambiguous problems over a safer conventional path
- most comfortable in small teams where engineering, product judgment, customer feedback, and ownership are closely connected
- optional personal line: **I have repeatedly chosen work where I had to learn the system from first principles rather than wait for a perfectly defined lane**

## 2. what I have worked on at Entire

**Verified on 2026-09-09:** 32 PRs · 12 merged · 18 open · 2 closed. First PR was in May; the deepest cluster of systems work has been August–September.

### main theme
Most of my work has ended up around **checkpoint/session correctness and Git integration** — especially where real repositories get messy: concurrency, interrupted processes, linked worktrees, incomplete transcripts, ref contention, malformed layouts, and backend migration.

The contribution arc is more useful than the PR count:

```text
checkpoint data quality
  → session crash consistency
  → agent/worktree ownership
  → canonical Git metadata identity
  → native atomic ref updates
  → storage batching and transcript snapshot consistency
```

### strongest contributions

#### #2211 — OPF ref updates — merged
- concurrency-safe ref updates using native Git compare-and-swap semantics
- TECH: concurrent writers, symbolic refs, cancellation, error classification
- key distinction to remember:
  - ordinary writes may be able to rebuild/retry after a conflict
  - OPF must reject a changed tip when that changes the meaning/base of the operation
- ★ strongest technical PR to discuss
- what I learned through review: an additional Entire lock felt safer initially, but Git's prepared transaction was the real correctness boundary; the extra lock added blocking without preventing a stale write
- concrete depth: files + reftable backends, symbolic-ref conversion races, exact Git error classification, cancellation after `commit: ok`, inherited Git environment isolation, and measured cost (~8.6 ms per ref update, below 1% of Stop-hook p50)

#### #2038 — duplicate session-end checkpoints — merged
- fixed duplicate checkpoint creation around session termination
- core problem: crash window between checkpoint publication and session bookkeeping
- durable ID reservation closes that window
- TECH: idempotency, crash consistency, recovery, commit trailers, backend migration
- note: substantial collaborator fixes/tests also landed here
- core design: persist the intended checkpoint ID before the checkpoint write, but do not advance "success" bookkeeping before storage succeeds
- ★ general lesson: **durable intent closes the duplicate window without opening a data-loss window**

#### #2241 + #2254 — canonical Git metadata resolution — merged
- established one canonical owner for `GitDir` / `CommonDir` / worktree identity
- migrated checkpoint consumers onto it
- TECH: linked worktrees, filesystem identity, malformed layouts, caching
- important design point: centralize metadata resolution without silently changing caller policy
- distinguished facts from policy: the resolver owns `GitDir`, `CommonDir`, and `WorktreeID`; each caller still decides whether failure is required, optional, or recoverable
- covered ordinary, linked, bare, separate-git-dir, submodule, reftable, symlink-alias, and malformed layouts

#### #2052 — Codex linked-worktree hooks — merged
- separated the hook/config file Entire owns from the file Codex actually discovers
- involved linked worktrees, config ownership, trust, and diagnostics
- accuracy note: merged version writes hooks locally with `os.WriteFile`; do **not** describe the earlier shared-write/locking design as shipped
- key product distinction: **where Codex discovers configuration is not necessarily a location Entire owns or may mutate**

#### #2099 — validated Claude Stop snapshots — open
- handles incomplete transcript writes + repeated Stop events
- ensures checkpoint data and derived accounting use the **same captured bytes**
- TECH: consistency while external agent state is still changing
- replaces "wait, then reopen a mutable file" with one owned snapshot whose bytes are validated and reused for storage, analysis, offsets, and finalization
- modern Stop payloads can prove readiness immediately; older payloads retain a bounded quiet-window fallback

### other shipped work worth knowing
- **#1937** — stop nested Git checkouts from polluting the parent session's file set and growing checkpoint metadata beyond GitHub's blob limit
- **#1969** — normalize/dedupe `files_touched` at the persistent write boundary; defense in depth even when every known producer should already dedupe
- **#1996** — my contribution was actionable OpenCode export-error reporting; broader fetching work was collaborative / landed through #1877
- **#2131** — storage batching groundwork; not every path is converted yet
- **#2192** — currently regression coverage after main overtook the production fix

- **#2099** — make Claude Stop capture operate on one validated transcript snapshot

- **#2285 + #2305 + #2320** — finish the staged migration to one canonical Git metadata resolver across session, strategy, hooks, settings, review, investigation, and trail consumers

## 4. previous work that connects naturally to Entire

### the overall collision

```text
Vibinex: infer useful context from Git history and code structure
Moss:    ingest, index, filter, rank, and retrieve information efficiently
Entire:  capture development context at creation time, bind it to Git,
         then make it searchable and usable by future humans and agents
```

★ Core answer:

> Entire feels less like a new domain and more like the convergence of the two domains I have already worked in. Vibinex taught me that a diff is not enough to understand a change. Moss taught me what it takes to ingest and retrieve useful information at scale. Entire captures the missing reasoning at the source, gives it durable Git provenance, and builds search, graph, review, and future agent workflows on top of it.

### Vibinex
- founding/product engineer in a three-person early-stage devtools startup; helped move from zero to 15+ customers
- built the **Git Profiler CLI in Rust**
- analyzed PRs / Git history to help teams understand changes and identify relevant reviewers
- worked on **syntactic diff graphs**, Git-blame relevance, authorship/reviewer signals
- built backend integrations around GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket
- designed privacy-conscious/on-prem processing when customers could not send source code to a hosted service
- worked directly with customers, so architecture and product feedback were never far apart
- recurring theme: **a code diff alone does not contain enough context to understand a change**
- ★ connection to Entire: Vibinex reconstructed context *after the fact* from code, blame, authorship, and repository history; Entire preserves much richer context *at creation time* and links it back to the same Git primitives

### Moss
- founding Rust/backend engineer working across Rust core, PyO3, Python/JS SDKs, and cloud ingestion services
- worked on an HNSW path for large embedding indexes, a compact binary embedding format, and bulk index creation through presigned object-store uploads
- shipped metadata filtering across Rust, PyO3, Python, and JS/TS surfaces, including comparison, set, boolean, and proximity operators
- found that post-filtering shallow `top_k` candidate lists destroyed hybrid-search recall; widened fusion depth, used union-based RRF, corrected score/filter ordering, and ran keyword/embedding branches in parallel
- measured filtered hybrid-search latency improving from roughly **88 ms → 17 ms on a 100k-document benchmark** while fixing empty-result quality failures
- built multi-document parsing/indexing and source-file tracking across doc-parser and index-manager flows
- moved embedding implementation and then orchestration toward Rust ownership: model download/cache, tokenization, ONNX inference, pooling, normalization, and session concurrency; verified numerical parity before deleting the Python implementation
- ★ connection to Entire: checkpoint history becomes a large, heterogeneous retrieval corpus; candidate recall, metadata filters, freshness, indexing ownership, latency, and honest partial results all matter
- accuracy note: this experience transfers directly to Entire Search concepts, but Entire's actual ANN/index implementation lives in backend repositories, not this CLI

### the three recurring engineering themes

1. **Provenance:** Vibinex asked who/what produced a change; Entire records the session and prompt that produced it.
2. **Retrieval:** Moss asked how to find the right information quickly and correctly; Entire Search asks that over code, commits, checkpoints, sessions, prompts, and transcripts.
3. **Trustworthy automation:** all three systems must distinguish absence from observation failure, preserve ownership boundaries, and recover honestly after interruption.

### recent platform / migration work
- worked across backend + infra + E2E workflows
- Java/Spring Boot + Next.js preview runtime / migration flows
- dealt with process lifecycle, health checks, ports, DB wiring, workspace VMs, Playwright E2E coverage
- also worked on code-review/eval behavior where **“no finding” must not accidentally mean “successful review”**
- connection: correctness under failure states / automation cannot collapse “failed to observe” into “nothing is wrong”

### Rust / systems
- EuroRust speaker: **“Production Unsafe Rust: Patterns for Zero-Copy Performance”**
- interested in systems, developer tools, low-level correctness, Git internals, and performance

Payload:
## Checkpoint persistence and sync: code-backed trace

### 1. Turn end → ephemeral checkpoint

- `handleLifecycleTurnEnd` copies the agent transcript into `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` after `agent.SanitizeTranscriptForStorage`; it backfills `prompt.txt`, merges transcript-derived file activity with Git status, excludes already-committed files, computes token usage, then calls `Strategy.SaveStep` with `StepContext` ([lifecycle.go:689](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go:689), [lifecycle.go:749](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go:749), [lifecycle.go:1008](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go:1008)).
- `ManualCommitStrategy.SaveStep` initializes/locks session state, migrates old shadow naming if needed, and dispatches `checkpoint.Step` to `EphemeralStore.Write`. Successful writes increment `StepCount`, prompt attribution, files touched, transcript start, and token windows ([manual_commit_git.go:27](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_git.go:27)).
- Shadow ref: `refs/heads/entire/<base-commit[:7]>-<sha256(worktree-id)[:6]>` ([ephemeral.go:717](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/ephemeral.go:717)).
- The first shadow commit is an orphan commit whose tree starts from current `HEAD`; later shadow commits parent the previous shadow tip. Thus it contains a complete code snapshot plus changed `.entire/metadata/<session>` files, without becoming ancestry of normal Git history ([ephemeral.go:62](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/ephemeral.go:62), [ephemeral.go:750](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/ephemeral.go:750)).
- Shadow commit trailers are:

  ```text
  Entire-Metadata: .entire/metadata/<session>
  Entire-Session: <session-id>
  Entire-Strategy: manual-commit
  ```

  Task steps use `Entire-Metadata-Task` instead ([trailers.go:156](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:156)).
- Writes are flocked plus compare-and-swap; identical trees are deduplicated. A status-budget breach is deliberately converted to a successful hook exit by turn-end bookkeeping ([ephemeral.go:113](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/ephemeral.go:113), [lifecycle.go:1052](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go:1052)).

### 2. User commit → persistent record

- `PrepareCommitMsg` finds eligible sessions and mints/reuses a checkpoint ID. Git-branch uses a random 12-lowercase-hex ID; git-refs uses a 26-character ULID. The only thing added to the normal code commit is:

  ```text
  Entire-Checkpoint: <checkpoint-id>
  ```

  Removing it opts the commit out. Merge/squash and Git sequence operations are not newly stamped; amend preserves/restores the existing ID ([manual_commit_hooks.go:323](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:323), [manual_commit_hooks.go:448](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:448), [trailers.go:234](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:234)).
- `PostCommit` parses that trailer, finds the same worktree/identity-linked sessions, applies the session-state transition, checks content/commit overlap, and invokes `CondenseSession`. No trailer means no persistent checkpoint; active sessions only have their base advanced ([manual_commit_hooks.go:908](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:908)).
- `CondenseSession` prefers the live transcript, falling back to the shadow copy. It filters `FilesTouched` to files in the actual commit, sanitizes → externalizes images → redacts, materializes subagent task records, computes attribution/summary, constructs `WriteOptions`, and writes `checkpoint.ReservedSession` ([manual_commit_condensation.go:515](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go:515), [manual_commit_condensation.go:632](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go:632)).
- `ReservedSession` is unconditional so every session sharing one checkpoint ID routes by that ID’s format to the same backend; per-session routing could split one checkpoint between branch and refs ([manual_commit_condensation.go:679](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go:679)).
- After success, state records `LastCheckpointID` and the exact normal commit SHA, resets the checkpoint/token/attribution window, advances `BaseCommit`, and either deletes the old shadow branch or carries remaining uncommitted agent changes into a new one ([manual_commit_hooks.go:1451](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:1451), [manual_commit_hooks.go:1527](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:1527)).

### 3. Persistent schema and hidden layouts

Both backends share `treeWriter`; only the anchoring ref/tree path differs ([store.go:17](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/store.go:17)).

Actual checkpoint subtree:

```text
metadata.json                    # CheckpointSummary
0/
  metadata.json                  # per-session Metadata
  full.jsonl[.NNN...]            # raw/sanitized/redacted, possibly chunked
  transcript.jsonl               # compact full session, best effort
  prompt.txt
  content_hash.txt               # sha256:<hex>
  assets/
    manifest.json
    <binary assets>
1/
  ...
tasks/<tool-use-id>/
  task.json
  agent-<agent-id>.jsonl         # absent when transcript unavailable
```

Important correction: implementation is zero-based (`0/`, `1/`), despite some API comments showing `1/` first ([persistent.go:539](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go:539), [persistent.go:569](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go:569)).

- Root `CheckpointSummary`: ID, strategy, branch, optional import anchor SHA, aggregate prompt/step count, files, session-path array, aggregate tokens/attribution, review/investigation/import flags ([metadata.go:531](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/api/checkpoint/metadata.go:531)).
- Session `Metadata`: session/agent/model/turn, timestamps, `SaveStepCount`, files, raw and compact transcript offsets, tokens, skill events, session metrics, initial attribution, prompt attribution diagnostics, summary and special-session fields ([metadata.go:387](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/api/checkpoint/metadata.go:387)).
- Transcript chunks use `full.jsonl`, `full.jsonl.001`, etc.; `content_hash.txt` enables idempotent backfill short-circuiting ([persistent.go:987](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go:987)).
- Persistent metadata commits have subject `Checkpoint: <id>` and trailers `Entire-Session`, `Entire-Strategy`, optionally `Entire-Agent`, `Ephemeral-branch` ([persistent.go:1275](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go:1275)).

Backend anchoring:

- Git-branch v1: `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1`; checkpoint subtree at `<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/`.
- Git-refs: `refs/entire/checkpoints/<id-last-2>/<full-id>`; the pointed commit’s tree root is the checkpoint subtree itself ([persistent_refs.go:28](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent_refs.go:28), [refs_naming.go:12](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_naming.go:12)).
- Normal history contains code plus the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, not transcripts. Shadow refs contain pending code snapshots and temporary metadata. Persistent branch/ref commits contain transcripts and metadata, not the normal code history.
- All persistent ref writes use per-ref flock + Git `update-ref` CAS and rebuild from the fresh tip on collision ([persistent_ref_update.go:84](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent_ref_update.go:84)).

### 4. Push, fetch, “pull,” and reconciliation

Git-branch:

- Pre-push sends `entire/checkpoints/v1` to the elected push remote or derived dedicated `checkpoint_remote`; it defers publishing a heads ref to an empty normal remote so the metadata branch cannot become the forge’s default branch ([manual_commit_push.go:51](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:51)).
- It pushes fast-forward-only. On failure it fetches, repairs disconnected history, replays local-only commits over the remote tip, and retries. Ordinary checkpoint push failures are fail-soft and do not block the user’s push; OPF abort/failure on the v1 path can abort it ([push_common.go:158](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/push_common.go:158)).
- Reads examine local v1 first, then elected-remote and legacy-origin tracking trees, selecting by checkpoint presence rather than merely branch existence. Only the elected remote may advance/replay the local primary; legacy origin is read-only fallback ([persistent.go:2165](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go:2165), [git_operations.go:397](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/git_operations.go:397)).

Git-refs:

- Every successful ref write enqueues `{"ref":"refs/entire/checkpoints/..."}` in `<git-common-dir>/entire-checkpoint-push-queue.jsonl`; the flocked queue survives interruptions and removes entries only after confirmed delivery ([pushqueue.go:20](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/pushqueue.go:20)).
- Pre-push batch-pushes queued refs fast-forward-only. On batch failure it retries each ref with fetch+replay; landed refs leave the queue, failed refs remain. It never force-pushes, and checkpoint-ref failures/OPF failures withhold metadata without blocking the user’s branch push ([manual_commit_push.go:366](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:366)).
- A missing specific ref is fetched on demand. User-facing list can opt into names-only `ls-remote refs/entire/checkpoints/*`; remote-only entries are ULID-timestamped stubs and hydrate lazily ([refs_store.go:373](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_store.go:373), [refs_store.go:493](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_store.go:493)).
- There is no checkpoint-specific “merge this during ordinary `git pull`” hook in this path. Foreground readers explicitly fetch v1 or individual checkpoint refs; push-time recovery synchronizes before retrying.

Common reconciliation:

- `ReconcileDisconnectedMetadataRef` handles the old empty-orphan/no-common-ancestor shape: ignore empty initialization commits, replay local data commits onto the remote tip, then advance local. Shared-ancestor divergence uses merge-base plus replay of local-only, non-merge commits. Remote history is preserved as ancestry; no force update is used ([metadata_reconcile.go:180](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/metadata_reconcile.go:180), [push_common.go:466](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/push_common.go:466)).

### Failure semantics worth preserving

- Hook paths are intentionally resilient: many discovery/open/condensation errors log and return success, preserving user commits and shadow data.
- Redaction failure drops the transcript rather than risk storing secrets; a checkpoint still writes if committed files/task content remain, otherwise it is skipped ([manual_commit_condensation.go:786](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go:786)).
- Corrupt session-slot mismatch fails closed rather than overwrite another session ([persistent.go:569](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go:569)).
- Git-refs enqueue occurs after the local ref write and is best-effort; if enqueue fails, the checkpoint exists locally but automatic push discovery can miss it ([refs_store.go:199](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_store.go:199)).
- Persistent mirrors are best-effort write-only; reads stay on primary. ID-kind routing keeps legacy hex checkpoints readable from v1 and ULIDs from git-refs during coexistence/migration ([open.go:74](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/open.go:74)).
